newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African rightist enraged over conviction.
newsitem.headline: South African rightist enraged over conviction.

text.p: White supremacist leader Eugene Terre' Blanche exploded with anger on Wednesday when a South African court convicted him of trying to murder a black employee and seriously assaulting another.

Dressed in grey camouflage and clutching a bush cap in his huge hand, he bent double and banged his fist on the dock as it became clear the magistrate would rule against him and then shot out of his seat when the guilty verdict was spoken.

"May God watch over you for what you have said. It will echo in the homes of every Boer (Afrikaner)," he bellowed at the magistrate. "The law, justice and God marks you. The struggle of the nation continues!"
Fighting back tears, he added in a breaking voice: "You are a traitor...the judgment is a political judgment."

Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB) supporters, women and men in khaki fatigues, cheered as their fiery leader charged out of the court, drowning out the magistrate who did not finish reading his ruling.
"Today the war has started," he told reporters outside the courtroom in Potchefstroom, west of Johannesburg.
But the defiant AWB leader later returned after a lunch adjournment.
Bail was set at 2,000 rand but was then reduced to 1,000 rand ($225) when a weeping Terre' Blanche said he was a "poor farmer with a wife and child".
The case was postponed to June 17 for sentencing and right-wingers, who packed the seats while blacks lined the walls of the courtroom, came up with the bail money within minutes.
One black man in court for the judgment said he did not believe Terre' Blanche was a political leader.
"This guy is not a politician, just a ruffian," he said.
Terre' Blanche, with a grey beard and gruff voice, rallied thousands of right-wingers behind the conservative cause during negotiations to end apartheid and bring democracy.

Terre' Blanche, 53, styled himself on Boer heroes who fought British colonialism at the turn of the last century. But he became the subject of derision after falling off his horse at a gathering in Pretoria some years ago.

His movement of swaggering, gun-toting neo-Nazis suffered a major blow when, in March 1994, a force of about 500 went into the former black homeland of Bophuthatswana in an ill-fated attempt to prop up its unpopular black homeland leader.
He like the right wing, was refusing to join the country's first all-race elections in April 1994, which brought to power Nelson Mandela's African National Congress.

The episode ended in about 50 deaths, including the killing of two rightists shot dead by a homeland soldier as they begged for mercy. Terre' Blanche, however, hailed the campaign as a "brilliant victory".
Stellenbosch University political analyst Jannie Gagiano thinks differently.
"Since Bophuthatswana, the AWB is no longer seen by Afrikaners as men with integrity...Now the image of brandy, Coke and paunches clings to them."
